storeCredit.title: Store Credit Management System
storeCredit.description: A production app that replaced a paper credit ledger with a real-time system the whole store staff relies on daily.
storeCredit.overview: My family runs a small neighborhood grocery store that, like many in Costa Rica, extends informal credit to regular customers, known locally as "fiado". For years that credit was tracked in a paper notebook: illegible handwriting, lost pages, no way to audit who wrote what or when, and no backup if the notebook itself got damaged.
storeCredit.problem: The notebook worked until it didn't. Balances got miscounted, entries got disputed, and there was no way for more than one person to update it at the same time without creating conflicting records. I built this app to solve that specific problem, not to build a generic point-of-sale system.
storeCredit.role: I designed, built and deployed the entire system alone: data model, front end, notification service and infrastructure, based on how the store staff actually work day to day.
storeCredit.architectureIntro: A React client talks to Firebase directly for reads and writes. A separate Node.js service, running continuously with PM2 on a machine at the store, listens for database changes and triggers outbound notifications.
features: Real-time sync: multiple staff members can log sales and payments at the same time and see updates instantly on every device.
A single shared Firebase Authentication account with a PIN-based profile selector, so every action stays tied to a specific person without individual logins.
Full audit trail: nothing is permanently deleted, every record keeps who created or edited it and when, and suspended accounts can be restored.
Daily summary broken down by payment method, with 80mm thermal receipt printing and one-tap copy for WhatsApp.
Automatic WhatsApp and email alerts sent to each customer on every transaction, handled by the separate notification service so the client app never blocks on it.
Automatic daily database backup to Google Cloud Storage.
storeCredit.screenshotsIntro: The real usage flow, with customer names, phone numbers and profile photos blurred. Amounts without an attached name aren't sensitive.

gallery.profileSelector: Profile selector: whoever is on shift picks their name and enters their PIN.
gallery.clientList: Customer list sorted by debt, with the store's total outstanding credit.
gallery.clientDetail: A customer's detail view: current debt, credit limit, history, and the buttons to log a purchase or payment.
gallery.dailySummary: Daily summary by payment method, used to balance the register at closing.
gallery.dailyMovements: Feed of every transaction for the day, in chronological order.

storeCredit.outcome: The app has fully replaced the paper ledger and is used every day by store staff, with zero infrastructure cost since it runs entirely on free-tier services.
storeCredit.stack: React, Vite, Firebase (Realtime Database, Authentication), Node.js, PM2, Vercel with continuous deployment from GitHub, Google Cloud Storage for backups.

alwaysBarca.title: Always Barça
alwaysBarca.description: 33 seasons. Multiple variables. One question: what actually explains FC Barcelona's successful seasons?
alwaysBarca.question: Does transfer spending predict FC Barcelona's sporting success better than other factors, like squad market value, coaching continuity, or academy player usage?
alwaysBarca.scope: 33 LaLiga seasons, from 1993/94 through 2025/26, split by coaching era (Guardiola, post-Messi, Xavi, Flick) so patterns from very different periods don't get diluted by mixing them together.
dataSources: datahub.io — historical LaLiga results back to the 1993-94 season
FBref — possession and xG per season, extracted with BeautifulSoup and Pandas
Kaggle and manual compilation — transfer spending and squad value, cross-validated by hand wherever automated coverage wasn't reliable
alwaysBarca.methodology: I tested five variables against each season's performance (net transfer spending, coaching continuity, La Masía academy minutes, squad market value, and coaching changes) using Pearson correlation and ANOVA, to separate what's statistically significant from what only looks like a trend. I was careful not to confuse correlation with causation: a bigger transfer budget in a given year can be a result of the club already being in a strong position, not the cause of the season that follows.
alwaysBarca.findings: Transfer spending and academy usage don't explain performance in a statistically significant way. Coaching continuity and squad market value do.
alwaysBarca.dashboardsIntro: Four linked dashboards on Tableau Public, each covering a different phase of the analysis.

overview.title: Performance, spending & coaching per season
overview.description: The starting point: how performance, net transfer spending and coaching changes move together across 33 seasons.

academy.title: Academy usage
academy.description: Minutes played by La Masía academy players per season, and whether that usage correlates with performance.

squadValue.title: Squad value
squadValue.description: Squad market value per season, one of the two variables that turned out to be statistically significant.

conclusions.title: Conclusions
conclusions.description: Results of the Pearson correlation and ANOVA across all five variables, with methodological limitations documented.

alwaysBarca.limitations: Data coverage is weaker for some 90s seasons, and a few seasons are statistical outliers because of off-field context (institutional crises, board changes) that no variable in this analysis captures. I'd rather state that plainly than let the results look more certain than they are.
alwaysBarca.stack: Python and Pandas for data collection and cleaning, SciPy for the statistical tests, Tableau Public for the four published dashboards.

messiOutlier.title: Messi: the statistically unrepeatable at World Cups
messiOutlier.description: Research in progress: comparing World Cup performance across four functional roles that are normally mutually exclusive.
messiOutlier.statusNote: No data has been collected yet and there is no dashboard. This page shows the full research outline; results will replace this note once the analysis exists.
messiOutlier.question: Is there a historical World Cup player who comes close to standing out across several mutually exclusive functional roles at once, or is that combination a true statistical outlier?
messiOutlier.thesis: The point isn't that Messi ranks first in every individual category, he doesn't: Mbappé ended up with more total World Cup goals after 2026. The point is that football demands roles with almost mutually exclusive skill sets, and what's statistically unusual is showing up in the top range of several different roles at the same time, not winning one category outright.
messiOutlier.rolesIntro: Functional roles, not fixed pitch positions, since the same player shifts position across a career.

roles.finisher: Finisher — converts chances into goals: goals, xG, shot conversion, shots on target.
roles.unbalancer: Unbalancer — creates individual danger by taking on defenders: successful dribbles, fouls drawn, progressive carries.
roles.playmaker: Playmaker — creates the direct chance: assists, key passes, xA, big chances created.
roles.orchestrator: Deep-lying orchestrator — circulates the ball and progresses the attack from deeper zones: progressive passes, completion rate, passes into the final third.

messiOutlier.comparisonPlayers: Cristiano Ronaldo, Neymar, Mbappé, Ronaldinho and Maradona, pending confirmation that 1986 World Cup data has the same level of statistical detail available.
dataSources: SofaScore — event-level stats documented back to the 1966 World Cup, no official API
FBref — reliable advanced metrics from the 2018 World Cup onward
Kaggle — base goal data per match and per tournament
messiOutlier.note: Reading this as proof that Messi is "underrated" is a personal reflection, not a conclusion the data itself supports. It's kept separate from the objective findings once they exist.
messiOutlier.stack: Python and Pandas planned for data collection, Tableau Public for a percentile-based scatter plot comparing all five players across the four roles.
